content: The combination of magnesium sulfate and potassium chloride increases the toxicity of senna through mechanisms that may lead to adverse effects. It is recommended to avoid this combination or use alternative medications. Co-administration of stimulant laxatives with sodium sulfate, magnesium sulfate, or potassium chloride can elevate the risk of mucosal ulceration or ischemic colitis. Similarly, the combination of senna with sodium sulfate, potassium chloride, magnesium sulfate, or polyethylene glycol can mutually increase toxicity, necessitating the avoidance of such combinations or the use of alternative treatments. Senna and deflazacort both reduce serum potassium levels, requiring careful monitoring and caution during use. Likewise, dichlorphenamide and senna also decrease serum potassium, necessitating similar precautions. Senna can increase the toxicity of digoxin due to potassium depletion, which raises the risk of cardiac toxicity. Similarly, senna increases the toxicity of lily of the valley, also due to potassium depletion, which can lead to cardiac complications. These interactions require close monitoring and caution. Psyllium can reduce the systemic absorption and therapeutic effects of intranasal metoclopramide when co-administered, as it impairs gastrointestinal motility. Patients should be monitored for reduced efficacy of metoclopramide. Psyllium also decreases the effects of sodium picosulfate through an unspecified interaction mechanism, though the clinical significance of this interaction is unclear. Electrolyte imbalances, particularly potassium loss, are potential side effects of senna. Other adverse effects include abdominal cramping, excessive bowel activity, flatulence, yellow-brown urine discoloration, melanosis coli, hypersensitivity reactions, gastrointestinal obstruction or perforation, ulcerative colitis, symptoms of appendicitis or acute surgical abdomen, fecal impaction, gastrointestinal bleeding, and rectal bleeding. Psyllium should be used cautiously in patients with esophageal strictures, stenosis, ulcers, swallowing difficulties, or intestinal adhesions, as it may predispose elderly patients to fecal impaction and bowel obstruction if fluid intake is insufficient. To prevent choking, psyllium must be taken with at least 8 ounces of fluid. It is not recommended for patients experiencing stomach pain. Senna is classified as pregnancy category C, while psyllium is category B. Lactating patients should use these medications with caution. Pregnant or breastfeeding individuals are advised to consult a healthcare professional before using over-the-counter drugs. In general, psyllium is considered acceptable during pregnancy, as controlled studies in pregnant women have shown no evidence of fetal risk.
